screens.title: Architectural Views and Documentation
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural documentation is the map and memory of a system. In this lesson you will learn why documentation is not paperwork but a practical tool for shared understanding, decision traceability, and future evolution. Good documentation helps new developers onboard quickly, helps operations provision and monitor systems, and preserves the rationale behind choices so the team can change direction confidently when needed. You'll discover a set of complementary "views" that capture different aspects: the logical structure, runtime behavior, development organization, physical deployment, and example scenarios that validate the design. We will also compare the 4+1 view model with a hierarchical alternative called the C4 model, and show the supporting artifacts that make documentation actionable—architectural decision records, glossaries, principles, and quality attribute scenarios. Finally, we'll cover common pitfalls and practical tips for keeping docs accurate and useful over time. By the end you'll be able to pick the right views for a stakeholder, write a concise ADR, and sketch context, container, and component diagrams that communicate essential structure without overwhelming readers. Consider: if you inherited a system today, what single diagram would save you a week of guesswork?

screens.title: What is Architectural Documentation?
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural documentation is a structured set of artifacts—diagrams, records, and short descriptions—that together describe a system's structure, behavior, and rationale. Its core purpose is threefold: to transfer knowledge between people, to record the reasons behind decisions, and to enable confident system evolution. A precise definition helps you choose what to document: the elements that are costly to rediscover, the decisions that are hard to reverse, and the interfaces that different teams depend on. A concrete example: if a service communicates via a message queue, documenting that dependency prevents an ops engineer from provisioning a database-only backup plan that misses queue retention settings. A common misconception is that documentation must be exhaustive; in practice, exhaustive documents become stale and unreadable. Instead, aim for “just enough” documentation—concise diagrams and ADRs for irreversible choices. Treat documentation like code: keep it in version control, review updates in pull requests, and link ADRs to PRs that implement the decision. Key takeaway: documentation that is versioned, concise, and tied to decisions stays useful; documentation that is long and unmanaged becomes a liability. What single high-cost-to-rediscover item would you write down first for your project?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Architectural documentation is a concise, versioned set of artifacts that capture structure, behavior, and rationale to support communication and evolution.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is Architectural Documentation?
Core Concept

Architectural Documentation

A concise, versioned collection of diagrams, decision records, and explanations that preserve system knowledge and rationale.

Why it matters
Prevents guesswork, speeds onboarding, and records trade-offs for future change.
Common mistake
Over-documenting everything instead of capturing high-impact, irreversible decisions.
Key Takeaway

Keep documentation short, versioned, and linked to the code and decisions it supports.

Analogy
Think of documentation like a map plus a lab notebook: the map shows where things are, while short records explain why you took a particular path.
Example scenario
A message queue dependency documented prevents a misconfiguration that would drop events during deployments.
Practical step
Write one ADR for a recent irreversible choice and link it to the implementation PR.
Check your understanding
  • Can you name one decision that would be expensive to rediscover?
  • Is there an existing ADR or diagram for that decision?

screens.title: Architectural Views: The Big Picture
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural views are different perspectives that highlight particular concerns of a system. No single view can capture everything, so architects assemble a set of complementary views to make distinct concerns visible. Think of a building: floor plans, wiring diagrams, and HVAC schematics each answer a different question. In software, common views are Logical, Process, Development, Physical (Deployment), and Scenario. The Logical View explains functional decomposition and is most useful to developers understanding responsibilities and boundaries. The Process View shows runtime behavior, concurrency, and communication patterns; operations and performance engineers rely on it to find bottlenecks. The Development View describes the organization of code into modules, libraries, and repositories—this helps build, test, and integrate. The Physical View maps software to hardware and networks and is vital for deployment, capacity planning, and reliability. The Scenario View stitches the others together using representative use cases to validate that the architecture satisfies requirements. A practical tip: choose views based on stakeholder questions. If the team asks, "How do we deploy and scale?" prioritize a deployment view. If they ask, "What are the service responsibilities?" produce a logical or container diagram. A common misconception is using the same diagram for all audiences; instead, tailor notation and detail to the audience. Which stakeholder question matters most for your current work?

keyIdea.title: Multiple perspectives
keyIdea.text: Use a collection of views to answer distinct stakeholder questions rather than a single overloaded diagram.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Architectural Views: The Big Picture
Overview

Why multiple views?

Each view surfaces a particular concern and serves specific stakeholders. Together, they form a coherent representation of the system.

Logical View
Functional decomposition for developers.
Process View
Runtime behavior, concurrency, and performance concerns.
Development View
Organization of code, builds, and integration points.
Physical / Deployment View
Mapping software onto hardware and networks.
Stakeholder mapping
Developers
Logical & Development views to understand responsibilities and code layout.
Operations
Physical and Process views for provisioning and monitoring.
Product / Designers
Scenario view to validate user flows and capabilities.
Architects
All views combined to reason about trade-offs and constraints.
Pro tip
Select the smallest set of views that answer a stakeholder's question; avoid using one diagram for all audiences.

screens.title: The 4+1 View Model Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The 4+1 View Model organizes architectural description into five complementary views. The Logical View shows the static structure—components, modules, and their relationships—to address functional requirements and developer understanding. The Process View captures runtime aspects such as concurrency, threads, inter-process communication, and sequencing; it helps design for performance and scalability. The Development View (sometimes called Implementation View) describes source code organization, packages, libraries, and the build structure so teams can manage code and integration. The Physical or Deployment View maps software pieces onto hardware, virtual machines, or cloud instances and makes network topology and data locality explicit. The plus-one is the Scenario View: representative use cases or user stories that show how elements from the other views cooperate to deliver functionality. Scenarios are crucial because they validate the architecture against real behaviors and quality attribute scenarios. Use this model by maintaining a small set of diagrams for each view and a few scenario narratives. A typical deliverable set might include a UML component diagram for Logical, a sequence or activity diagram for Process, a repository structure snapshot for Development, a deployment diagram for Physical, and three scenario narratives that exercise key flows. A common misuse is to create many diagrams with inconsistent notation; instead, choose consistent notation and link diagrams to ADRs and code where possible.

keyIdea.title: 4+1 summary
keyIdea.text: The 4+1 model provides five complementary views that together validate that the system meets both functional and non-functional requirements.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › The 4+1 View Model Explained

4+1 Views — concise set

Each view answers a different question and together they validate the architecture.

Logical View
Functional decomposition and component relationships for developers.
Process View
Runtime behavior, interactions, and concurrency for performance planning.
Development View
Repository, modules, and build structure for maintainers.
Physical View
Mapping software onto hosts, networks, and storage for operations.
Scenario View

Validating the architecture with use cases

Scenarios exercise the other views. They show how components interact in practice and reveal gaps in design.

Example scenario
User uploads a photo, API stores metadata, publishes an event, and an async processor applies a filter then writes to object storage.
Deliverable set
One diagram per view plus 2–4 scenario narratives is usually sufficient for medium systems.
Key Takeaway

Use the 4+1 set as a checklist—document views that reveal important trade-offs and behaviors.

screens.title: Deep Dive: Logical View
screens.narratorSegment: The Logical View focuses on the system's functional decomposition. It shows the key abstractions, components, and their relationships so developers can understand responsibilities and boundaries. This view often uses component or class diagrams. A practical example drawn from the chapter: a User Service class that depends on a repository and an authentication service. Documenting this relationship clarifies where data validation happens and which component owns state. A common misconception is that the logical view must map one-to-one to deployment units. In reality, a logical component may be implemented across multiple processes or services; the mapping is intentionally abstract. When you create a logical view, name components by responsibility, show key interfaces, and annotate important constraints such as consistency or transaction boundaries. Also link each component to the relevant ADRs and the code location in the Development View. This linking turns static diagrams into navigable knowledge: you can go from a box on a diagram to the ADR explaining a trade-off and to the repository that contains the implementation. As a takeaway, practice by sketching the logical components for a small service and listing one responsibility per component — clarity beats completeness.

keyIdea.title: Logical view focus
keyIdea.text: Describe components by responsibility and show interfaces; avoid conflating logical boundaries with runtime or deployment units.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Deep Dive: Logical View
Definition

Logical View

Shows functional decomposition, components, and responsibilities to help developers understand the system's conceptual organization.

Naming guideline
Name components by responsibility, not by implementation detail.
Link to code
Annotate boxes with repository paths or ADR references to make diagrams actionable.
Concrete Example
# Logical Component: User Service
class UserService:
  def __init__(self, user_repository, auth_service):
    self.user_repository = user_repository  # Dependency on Data Access Component
    self.auth_service = auth_service        # Dependency on Authentication Component

  def create_user(self, user_data):
    # Business logic for creating a user
    pass

  def get_user(self, user_id):
    # Retrieve user from repository
    pass
This Python snippet represents logical components and their dependencies; the diagram would show boxes for UserService, UserRepository, and AuthService with arrows indicating dependencies.
Key Takeaway
Logical views clarify responsibilities and interfaces; annotate them with code links and ADRs to keep them actionable.

screens.title: Deep Dive: Process View
screens.narratorSegment: The Process View describes how the system behaves at runtime: which processes or threads exist, how they communicate, and where concurrency or distributed processing occurs. This view addresses non-functional goals like performance, scalability, and resilience. Use sequence diagrams or activity diagrams to show how requests flow across services, which components run in separate processes, and where asynchronous messaging occurs. For example, in the photo-processing system the A P I publishes a message to a queue and an image processor consumes it asynchronously; a Process View will highlight this decoupling and help you reason about throughput and retry behavior. A common pitfall is ignoring failure paths—include timeouts, backoff, and queue overflow scenarios in your diagrams. Another useful practice is annotating expected load or latency targets on critical paths to inform capacity planning. The Process View is particularly valuable when teams design scaling strategies or need to discover bottlenecks. As a practical exercise, sketch a sequence where a user uploads a file and the system publishes an event; then annotate where you would add monitoring and retries. Ending question: which runtime path in your system is most sensitive to latency and deserves an explicit process diagram?

keyIdea.text: Model runtime flows, concurrency, and failure-handling to design for performance and reliability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Deep Dive: Process View
Process View

Runtime behavior and flows

Show processes, message flows, and runtime interactions to reason about performance, scaling, and resilience.

Include failure paths
Annotate retries, timeouts, and queue overflow to surface operational risks.
Annotate load
Add expected throughput or latency numbers on critical paths for capacity planning.
Example: Photo upload flow
User uploads a photo → API accepts metadata and stores raw file → API publishes event to queue → Image processor consumes event and writes processed image to object storage.
Where to monitor
Queue depth, processing latency, and API request latencies are natural monitoring points.
Check your understanding
Identify an async boundary in your system and list three failure modes to document.
Key Takeaway
Model runtime flows, include failure paths, and annotate load to make process diagrams operationally useful.

screens.title: Development View (Implementation)
screens.narratorSegment: The Development View describes how the system is organized for developers: packages, repositories, libraries, and the modular structure used during implementation. It helps teams manage builds, dependencies, and integration. For instance, a monorepo may group services together but use folder boundaries to keep code modular, while a polyrepo approach separates services into different repositories. The Development View should make it easy to answer questions such as where to find a component's code, which packages are shared, and how builds are composed. Include details like repository structure, CI/CD pipeline references, and key library versions where they influence compatibility. A common misconception is to omit cross-cutting concerns; instead annotate places where shared libraries or common middleware are used. Linking Development View artifacts to ADRs is crucial: if an ADR chose a database or a messaging pattern, document where that configuration lives in the repository. For maintainability, store diagrams and short READMEs near the code and update them as part of pull requests. As a practical step, create a short README for one repository that explains its role and where it appears in the logical and deployment views.

keyIdea.title: Development view purpose
keyIdea.text: Show code organization, repository layout, and build references so teams can find, change, and integrate code confidently.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Development View (Implementation)
Implementation perspective

Development View

Document repository layout, module boundaries, and build or packaging details to help developers navigate and maintain code.

Repository guidance
Add a short README that explains the repository's role and links to diagrams and ADRs.
CI/CD references
Point to pipeline configuration and build artifacts that implement architectural choices.
Concrete example
If a service depends on a shared library, show where that library lives, its version policy, and which repositories consume it. This prevents accidental incompatible upgrades.
Key Takeaway
Keep development artifacts close to code and document integration points so teams can change code with confidence.
Check your understanding
Locate a module you changed recently and verify there is a README and an ADR for any irreversible choice you made.

screens.title: Deep Dive: Physical / Deployment View
screens.narratorSegment: The Physical or Deployment View maps software components onto hardware and network topologies. It makes explicit where services run, how data is stored, and how network connections cross trust or failure boundaries. This view is essential for capacity planning, reliability engineering, and operations. For example, documenting that the image processor runs in a separate availability zone and that metadata is stored in a managed relational database highlights operational trade-offs like latency and failover cost. When creating a deployment view, include hosts, virtual machines, containers, load balancers, firewalls, and storage endpoints, and annotate important constraints such as data residency or network bottlenecks. A key practice is to connect the deployment view to monitoring, indicating which metrics and alerts correspond to which deployed component. Avoid a common mistake: assuming a deployment view is static. With infrastructure as code, deployments change frequently, so keep the view in version control and update it alongside infrastructure changes. Final question: what is one deployment constraint in your system that should be surfaced in a diagram today? Deep Dive: Physical / Deployment View means show where components run and how they connect at the network level to support operations and capacity decisions.. In practical terms, mapping software to hardware, networks, and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Show where components run and how they connect at the network level to support operations and capacity decisions.

content.html:

Deployment concerns

Physical / Deployment View

Maps software onto compute, network, and storage to show where components run and how they communicate across boundaries.

Annotate constraints
Show data residency, availability zones, and network segments that affect reliability and compliance.
Link to monitoring
Indicate which metrics and alerts map to deployed nodes to speed troubleshooting.
Concrete example
Document that the image processor runs in a separate availability zone and that object storage is in a managed service; this highlights failover and latency trade-offs.

Check your understanding

screens.title: Scenario View and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: The Scenario View uses representative use cases or user stories to show how elements from other views work together to deliver functionality. Scenarios are the bridge between static diagrams and real behavior: they validate that the logical, process, and deployment choices actually satisfy requirements. A practical scenario for the photo app is: a user uploads a photo, the backend stores metadata and publishes an event, the processor applies filters, and the processed image is returned or shared. Writing this scenario forces you to name the components involved and to examine failure modes: what happens when the processor is slow, when the queue is full, or when storage is unavailable? Scenario narratives should include the steps, the expected quality attributes (for instance a 95th percentile latency target), and the failure-handling approach. A misconception is to treat scenarios as tests; while they inform tests, their primary role is architectural validation and communication. Create 2–4 scenarios that exercise the most critical or risky parts of your system. Each scenario becomes a checklist: diagram the elements, call out the key non-functional requirements, and link to ADRs that affect the scenario. Ask yourself: which scenario would break first under load and why?

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Scenario View and Use Cases
Scenario View

Use cases to validate design

Write short narratives describing steps, expected outcomes, and failure modes to ensure the architecture supports real behavior.

Example: Photo upload scenario
User uploads → API stores metadata → API publishes event → Processor applies filter → Processed image stored and delivered.
Checklist
  • Name involved components and views required to implement the scenario.
  • Document key quality attributes such as latency, throughput, and reliability targets.
  • Enumerate failure modes and mitigation approaches.
Key Takeaway
Scenarios connect diagrams to behavior; they reveal hidden assumptions and validate design trade-offs.

screens.title: C4 Model: Context → Containers → Components → Code
screens.narratorSegment: The C4 Model provides a hierarchical way to describe architecture by zooming in from high-level context down to code. Level one, the System Context Diagram, shows the system boundaries, users, and external systems. This answers the question: what is in scope and who interacts with it? Level two, Container Diagrams, break the system into major deployable applications, data stores, and services—this is a practical bridge between logical components and deployment concerns. Level three, Component Diagrams, zoom into a single container showing its internal parts and interactions. Level four, Code Diagrams, are optional and show classes or files within a component when useful. Use the C4 approach when you need a clear, layered narrative: start with context for stakeholders who need the big picture, then provide container and component views for developers and operators. A useful practice is to maintain one diagram per C4 level for important parts of the system and link each container to its deployment and ADRs. A common error is mixing levels on one diagram; keep each level focused so readers can follow a single abstraction at a time. Which part of your project would benefit most from a container-level view?

keyIdea.text: C4 offers a zoom-in hierarchy from context to code so you can present the right level of detail to each audience.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › C4 Model: Context → Containers → Components → Code

C4 Model levels

A pragmatic hierarchy: Context, Container, Component, optional Code diagrams.

System Context (C1)
Shows system boundary and external actors.
Container (C2)
Major deployable applications and data stores inside the system.
Component (C3)
Internal parts of a container and their interactions.
Practical guidance
Keep diagrams per level focused. Link containers to deployment documentation and ADRs. Use context diagrams to onboard non-technical stakeholders quickly.
Common mistake
Mixing levels causes confusion—don't show classes on a context diagram or expect product owners to read component-level detail.
Check your understanding
Pick one container and list the components you would show at C3 to implement a core use case.

screens.title: Supporting Artifacts: ADRs, Glossary, and Principles
screens.narratorSegment: Effective documentation goes beyond diagrams. Architectural Decision Records, or ADRs, capture one decision per file: the context, alternatives considered, the chosen option, and consequences. ADRs answer the question "why" and are invaluable when revisiting trade-offs. A glossary provides a shared vocabulary so terms like "user session" or "event" are unambiguous across teams. Architectural principles are short, high-level guidelines—examples include "favor loose coupling" or "design for failure"—that steer choices consistently. Also record your technology stack and quality attribute scenarios: which technologies are used, which versions, and scenarios that define how the system should perform. A concrete ADR example would document why a team chose Kafka for messaging: list alternatives, explain throughput or ordering requirements, and note operational implications. Avoid creating an ADR for trivial choices; prioritize decisions that are hard to reverse or affect many teams. Finally, put these artifacts in version control, reference them from diagrams, and update them as part of the change process. This turns architecture documentation into living knowledge rather than archival text. Which recent decision in your team should have been recorded as an ADR? In practical terms, what to record beyond diagrams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:

ADRs

Short files documenting one architectural decision: context, alternatives, decision, and consequences.

When to write an ADR
For choices that are hard to reverse or affect multiple teams: new messaging technology, data model changes, or deployment strategies.
Other artifacts
  • Glossary: shared vocabulary for ambiguous terms.
  • Architectural principles: short guidelines that steer decisions.
  • Technology stack and quality attribute scenarios.
Practical tip
Store ADRs and glossaries in the same repository as code and reference them from diagrams and PRs so they evolve together.

screens.title: Keeping Documentation Useful: Best Practices and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Good documentation practices emphasize clarity, concision, and maintainability. Treat documentation like code: keep it in version control, review changes as part of pull requests, and automate checks when possible. Aim for "just enough" documentation—capture high-impact diagrams and ADRs rather than exhaustive prose that becomes stale. Prioritize documenting irreversible decisions and areas of complexity. Link diagrams to code paths and ADRs so readers can navigate from a visual to implementation and rationale. Avoid two common mistakes: over-documenting with long, rarely-read documents, and under-documenting where critical decisions are unrecorded. Both harm teams. Make updates part of the workflow: add ADR updates to the definition-of-done for relevant PRs and schedule brief documentation reviews during maintenance windows. Encourage a culture where small, frequent updates keep documentation current. A practical habit is to create a template ADR and a container diagram starter in the repository so teams can easily create and update artifacts. Final reflective question: what small change to your team's workflow would make documentation a natural byproduct of development instead of an extra task? Best practices

fullNarratorScript:
Architectural documentation is the map and memory of a system. In this lesson you will learn why documentation is not paperwork but a practical tool for shared understanding, decision traceability, and future evolution. Good documentation helps new developers onboard quickly, helps operations provision and monitor systems, and preserves the rationale behind choices so the team can change direction confidently when needed. You'll discover a set of complementary "views" that capture different aspects: the logical structure, runtime behavior, development organization, physical deployment, and example scenarios that validate the design. We will also compare the 4+1 view model with a hierarchical alternative called the C4 model, and show the supporting artifacts that make documentation actionable—architectural decision records, glossaries, principles, and quality attribute scenarios. Finally, we'll cover common pitfalls and practical tips for keeping docs accurate and useful over time. By the end you'll be able to pick the right views for a stakeholder, write a concise ADR, and sketch context, container, and component diagrams that communicate essential structure without overwhelming readers. Consider: if you inherited a system today, what single diagram would save you a week of guesswork?

In this first objectives slide we set clear, practical goals. You will be able to explain the purpose and importance of architectural documentation, which means articulating how diagrams and records preserve institutional knowledge and reduce onboarding time. You will describe different architectural views — that is, the Logical, Process, Development, Physical, and Scenario views from the 4+1 model — and explain which stakeholder each view serves. You will also understand how to use views to communicate complexity, translating architecture into concrete diagrams that answer a stakeholder's question. Finally you will identify best practices for creating maintainable documentation: keep records concise, store them with the code, and update them as decisions change. Each objective connects to a practical milestone: write an ADR, sketch a container diagram, and pair a deployment sketch with a runbook. These outcomes help you move from abstract theory to artifacts that teams actually use. Think about one project you know and which of these four objectives would have the most immediate impact.

In this second objectives slide we connect learning to practical actions. When you explain documentation's purpose, aim to cite a concrete benefit such as reduced onboarding time or fewer production incidents caused by misunderstandings. For describing views, practice by selecting one stakeholder—developers, ops, or product—and produce a single diagram that answers their most urgent question. To use views to communicate complexity, practice a small deliverable: a two-page package with a context diagram and one container diagram plus a short ADR that records a key choice. For best practices, adopt a habit: store diagrams and ADRs in the same repository as the code, review them in PRs, and prune or update entries during sprints. These actions convert abstract objectives into milestones you can check off. The intention is not to produce endless text but to create bite-sized, versioned artifacts that teams will actually read and use. Which of these actions could you try in your next sprint to make architecture visible and maintainable?

Architectural documentation is a structured set of artifacts—diagrams, records, and short descriptions—that together describe a system's structure, behavior, and rationale. Its core purpose is threefold: to transfer knowledge between people, to record the reasons behind decisions, and to enable confident system evolution. A precise definition helps you choose what to document: the elements that are costly to rediscover, the decisions that are hard to reverse, and the interfaces that different teams depend on. A concrete example: if a service communicates via a message queue, documenting that dependency prevents an ops engineer from provisioning a database-only backup plan that misses queue retention settings. A common misconception is that documentation must be exhaustive; in practice, exhaustive documents become stale and unreadable. Instead, aim for “just enough” documentation—concise diagrams and ADRs for irreversible choices. Treat documentation like code: keep it in version control, review updates in pull requests, and link ADRs to PRs that implement the decision. Key takeaway: documentation that is versioned, concise, and tied to decisions stays useful; documentation that is long and unmanaged becomes a liability. What single high-cost-to-rediscover item would you write down first for your project?

Architectural views are different perspectives that highlight particular concerns of a system. No single view can capture everything, so architects assemble a set of complementary views to make distinct concerns visible. Think of a building: floor plans, wiring diagrams, and HVAC schematics each answer a different question. In software, common views are Logical, Process, Development, Physical (Deployment), and Scenario. The Logical View explains functional decomposition and is most useful to developers understanding responsibilities and boundaries. The Process View shows runtime behavior, concurrency, and communication patterns; operations and performance engineers rely on it to find bottlenecks. The Development View describes the organization of code into modules, libraries, and repositories—this helps build, test, and integrate. The Physical View maps software to hardware and networks and is vital for deployment, capacity planning, and reliability. The Scenario View stitches the others together using representative use cases to validate that the architecture satisfies requirements. A practical tip: choose views based on stakeholder questions. If the team asks, "How do we deploy and scale?" prioritize a deployment view. If they ask, "What are the service responsibilities?" produce a logical or container diagram. A common misconception is using the same diagram for all audiences; instead, tailor notation and detail to the audience. Which stakeholder question matters most for your current work?

The 4+1 View Model organizes architectural description into five complementary views. The Logical View shows the static structure—components, modules, and their relationships—to address functional requirements and developer understanding. The Process View captures runtime aspects such as concurrency, threads, inter-process communication, and sequencing; it helps design for performance and scalability. The Development View (sometimes called Implementation View) describes source code organization, packages, libraries, and the build structure so teams can manage code and integration. The Physical or Deployment View maps software pieces onto hardware, virtual machines, or cloud instances and makes network topology and data locality explicit. The plus-one is the Scenario View: representative use cases or user stories that show how elements from the other views cooperate to deliver functionality. Scenarios are crucial because they validate the architecture against real behaviors and quality attribute scenarios. Use this model by maintaining a small set of diagrams for each view and a few scenario narratives. A typical deliverable set might include a UML component diagram for Logical, a sequence or activity diagram for Process, a repository structure snapshot for Development, a deployment diagram for Physical, and three scenario narratives that exercise key flows. A common misuse is to create many diagrams with inconsistent notation; instead, choose consistent notation and link diagrams to ADRs and code where possible.

The Logical View focuses on the system's functional decomposition. It shows the key abstractions, components, and their relationships so developers can understand responsibilities and boundaries. This view often uses component or class diagrams. A practical example drawn from the chapter: a User Service class that depends on a repository and an authentication service. Documenting this relationship clarifies where data validation happens and which component owns state. A common misconception is that the logical view must map one-to-one to deployment units. In reality, a logical component may be implemented across multiple processes or services; the mapping is intentionally abstract. When you create a logical view, name components by responsibility, show key interfaces, and annotate important constraints such as consistency or transaction boundaries. Also link each component to the relevant ADRs and the code location in the Development View. This linking turns static diagrams into navigable knowledge: you can go from a box on a diagram to the ADR explaining a trade-off and to the repository that contains the implementation. As a takeaway, practice by sketching the logical components for a small service and listing one responsibility per component — clarity beats completeness.

The Process View describes how the system behaves at runtime: which processes or threads exist, how they communicate, and where concurrency or distributed processing occurs. This view addresses non-functional goals like performance, scalability, and resilience. Use sequence diagrams or activity diagrams to show how requests flow across services, which components run in separate processes, and where asynchronous messaging occurs. For example, in the photo-processing system the A P I publishes a message to a queue and an image processor consumes it asynchronously; a Process View will highlight this decoupling and help you reason about throughput and retry behavior. A common pitfall is ignoring failure paths—include timeouts, backoff, and queue overflow scenarios in your diagrams. Another useful practice is annotating expected load or latency targets on critical paths to inform capacity planning. The Process View is particularly valuable when teams design scaling strategies or need to discover bottlenecks. As a practical exercise, sketch a sequence where a user uploads a file and the system publishes an event; then annotate where you would add monitoring and retries. Ending question: which runtime path in your system is most sensitive to latency and deserves an explicit process diagram?

The Development View describes how the system is organized for developers: packages, repositories, libraries, and the modular structure used during implementation. It helps teams manage builds, dependencies, and integration. For instance, a monorepo may group services together but use folder boundaries to keep code modular, while a polyrepo approach separates services into different repositories. The Development View should make it easy to answer questions such as where to find a component's code, which packages are shared, and how builds are composed. Include details like repository structure, CI/CD pipeline references, and key library versions where they influence compatibility. A common misconception is to omit cross-cutting concerns; instead annotate places where shared libraries or common middleware are used. Linking Development View artifacts to ADRs is crucial: if an ADR chose a database or a messaging pattern, document where that configuration lives in the repository. For maintainability, store diagrams and short READMEs near the code and update them as part of pull requests. As a practical step, create a short README for one repository that explains its role and where it appears in the logical and deployment views.

The Physical or Deployment View maps software components onto hardware and network topologies. It makes explicit where services run, how data is stored, and how network connections cross trust or failure boundaries. This view is essential for capacity planning, reliability engineering, and operations. For example, documenting that the image processor runs in a separate availability zone and that metadata is stored in a managed relational database highlights operational trade-offs like latency and failover cost. When creating a deployment view, include hosts, virtual machines, containers, load balancers, firewalls, and storage endpoints, and annotate important constraints such as data residency or network bottlenecks. A key practice is to connect the deployment view to monitoring, indicating which metrics and alerts correspond to which deployed component. Avoid a common mistake: assuming a deployment view is static. With infrastructure as code, deployments change frequently, so keep the view in version control and update it alongside infrastructure changes. Final question: what is one deployment constraint in your system that should be surfaced in a diagram today? Deep Dive: Physical / Deployment View means show where components run and how they connect at the network level to support operations and capacity decisions.. In practical terms, mapping software to hardware, networks, and storage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Scenario View uses representative use cases or user stories to show how elements from other views work together to deliver functionality. Scenarios are the bridge between static diagrams and real behavior: they validate that the logical, process, and deployment choices actually satisfy requirements. A practical scenario for the photo app is: a user uploads a photo, the backend stores metadata and publishes an event, the processor applies filters, and the processed image is returned or shared. Writing this scenario forces you to name the components involved and to examine failure modes: what happens when the processor is slow, when the queue is full, or when storage is unavailable? Scenario narratives should include the steps, the expected quality attributes (for instance a 95th percentile latency target), and the failure-handling approach. A misconception is to treat scenarios as tests; while they inform tests, their primary role is architectural validation and communication. Create 2–4 scenarios that exercise the most critical or risky parts of your system. Each scenario becomes a checklist: diagram the elements, call out the key non-functional requirements, and link to ADRs that affect the scenario. Ask yourself: which scenario would break first under load and why?

The C4 Model provides a hierarchical way to describe architecture by zooming in from high-level context down to code. Level one, the System Context Diagram, shows the system boundaries, users, and external systems. This answers the question: what is in scope and who interacts with it? Level two, Container Diagrams, break the system into major deployable applications, data stores, and services—this is a practical bridge between logical components and deployment concerns. Level three, Component Diagrams, zoom into a single container showing its internal parts and interactions. Level four, Code Diagrams, are optional and show classes or files within a component when useful. Use the C4 approach when you need a clear, layered narrative: start with context for stakeholders who need the big picture, then provide container and component views for developers and operators. A useful practice is to maintain one diagram per C4 level for important parts of the system and link each container to its deployment and ADRs. A common error is mixing levels on one diagram; keep each level focused so readers can follow a single abstraction at a time. Effective documentation goes beyond diagrams. Architectural Decision Records, or ADRs, capture one decision per file: the context, alternatives considered, the chosen option, and consequences. ADRs answer the question "why" and are invaluable when revisiting trade-offs. A glossary provides a shared vocabulary so terms like "user session" or "event" are unambiguous across teams. Architectural principles are short, high-level guidelines—examples include "favor loose coupling" or "design for failure"—that steer choices consistently. Also record your technology stack and quality attribute scenarios: which technologies are used, which versions, and scenarios that define how the system should perform. A concrete ADR example would document why a team chose Kafka for messaging: list alternatives, explain throughput or ordering requirements, and note operational implications. Avoid creating an ADR for trivial choices; prioritize decisions that are hard to reverse or affect many teams. Finally, put these artifacts in version control, reference them from diagrams, and update them as part of the change process. Good documentation practices emphasize clarity, concision, and maintainability. Treat documentation like code: keep it in version control, review changes as part of pull requests, and automate checks when possible. Aim for "just enough" documentation—capture high-impact diagrams and ADRs rather than exhaustive prose that becomes stale. Prioritize documenting irreversible decisions and areas of complexity. Link diagrams to code paths and ADRs so readers can navigate from a visual to implementation and rationale. Avoid two common mistakes: over-documenting with long, rarely-read documents, and under-documenting where critical decisions are unrecorded. Both harm teams. Make updates part of the workflow: add ADR updates to the definition-of-done for relevant PRs and schedule brief documentation reviews during maintenance windows. Encourage a culture where small, frequent updates keep documentation current. These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, architectural documentation is a practical tool: concise, versioned artifacts support onboarding, operations, and future change. Second, architectural views are complementary: use Logical, Process, Development, Physical, and Scenario views (the 4+1 model) or a hierarchical C4 approach to present the right level of detail to each stakeholder. Third, supporting artifacts like ADRs, glossaries, and quality attribute scenarios capture the rationale and constraints that diagrams alone cannot. Keep these artifacts close to the code and update them as part of normal development workflows so documentation remains a living resource.
